words.etymology:
Uncertain. Most credibly akin to ënjtem (“to fill up, swell from eating”), dialectally enj, ënj ~ âj (“to cause to swell”), in reference to Fat Thursday, as proposed by Topalli (2017).
Outdated theories
Treimer (1923) assumes the existence of a pagan god *Enji, which must have been the most important, given how it was used to calque Juppiter, akin to Sanskrit अग्नि (agni), Hindu god of fire. This is endorsed by Orel (1998).
Oštir (1925) tentatively connects to Etruscan 𐌀𐌉𐌔 (ais, “god”) or to 𐌖𐌍𐌉 (uni, “Juno”).
Mjeda (1932) derives it from Ancient Greek ἕνη (hénē), comparing its use in the expression Ancient Greek ἕνη καὶ νέα (hénē kaì néa, “the last day of the month”).

words.etymology:
From Proto-Albanian *lutśi-, from the Proto-Indo-European root *lewt-, *lewdʰ- (“song, sound”), from Proto-Indo-European *lew- (“to sound, resound, sing out”). Cognate to Latin laudo (“to praise”) and others. Alternatively, from Proto-Indo-European *lewd- (“to duck; feign”). Compare Proto-Germanic *lutōną (“to conceal”) (whence English lote, Gothic 𐌻𐌿𐍄𐍉𐌽 (lutōn, “cheat, deceive”)), Lithuanian liūstù (“to be sad”).
Alternatively, from Proto-Albanian *lugtja, from Proto-Indo-European *lewgʰ- (“to lie, tell falsehood”), with the same semantic shift "tell lies" > "request" found in Baltic cognates such as Latvian lūgt (“to ask, request”).
